faq.a: Friction is a force that pushes against sliding when two surfaces rub. It comes from tiny bumps catching and from molecules sticking together. Without it you couldn't walk, hold a cup or stop a bike.

faq.q: Why is there water on top of ice?
faq.a: The molecules at the surface of ice have fewer neighbours holding them in place, so they jiggle loosely and form a thin, liquid-like layer just a few molecules thick. Sliding also warms the ice by friction, adding more meltwater.
asks: What makes the surface of ice wet?

faq.q: Is very cold ice less slippery?
faq.a: Yes. At very low temperatures, such as minus 30 degrees Celsius, the slippery surface layer is much thinner, so ice becomes surprisingly grippy. Skaters prefer ice just a few degrees below freezing.
asks: Why is ice most slippery near zero degrees?

faq.q: Do skates melt the ice by pressing on it?
faq.a: That was the old explanation, but a skater's pressure lowers the melting point by only a fraction of a degree. The real reasons are the loose surface layer and the heat from friction as the blade slides.
asks: Is pressure melting why skates glide?

faq.q: Why do people put grit on icy paths?
faq.a: Grit adds rough particles that catch on shoes and tyres, giving back friction. Salt helps too, because it lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so the ice melts.
asks: Why do we salt icy roads?

facts: Ice is most slippery a few degrees below 0 degrees Celsius; at much lower temperatures it becomes less slippery.
Michael Faraday suggested in 1850 that ice has a thin liquid-like layer on its surface.

quiz.say: Which ice is the most slippery?
quiz.why: Near its melting point, ice has the thickest watery surface layer, so friction is lowest.

wrong.0: Very cold ice has a thinner surface layer and is actually grippier.
wrong.2: How slippery ice is depends strongly on its temperature.
